utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Usher, please have the accused brought in. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I suppose everybody is ready, are the interpreters ready? These booths have been working since this morning if I am not mistaken, so I suppose everything is working just perfectly. Thank you. Everybody hears me? Good afternoon. All right, we can now resume. We will have Ms. Smaila Sahman brought in again now. Mr. Harmon, I think you had a few questions you want to ask her; is that not right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President and your Honours. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The witness spoke for quite a long time, she was very clear. I think you are only going to ask for some clarifications that you were going to ask. You are not going to have her repeat everything, are you? I am counting on you, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You can depend on me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Now you have the sword of Damocles hanging over your head. The number of days is that sword. If you want to hear one witness for 60 days, you can do that. It is as you like. (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Ms. Sahman, do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Were you able to rest a bit after having spoken for so long yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. We have not finished with the examination. I believe the Prosecutor is going to ask you several questions for clarifying some of the points in your testimony for the benefit of the judges. Mr. Harmon, the floor is yours. MS. SMAILA SAHMAN (continued)

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Sahman.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you some questions that will more sharply focus on some parts of your testimony. Let me begin by referring you to the event when the HVO police came to your house on 24th January 1993, and asked your husband for weapons. Can you describe to the court how those men who came to your house were dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were dressed in camouflage uniforms with the HVO insignia. They had the chequer boards on their hats, and they introduced themselves as the HVO police.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Ms. Sahman, you indicated throughout your testimony that the people who came to your house were looking for a sniper rifle. Did you ever see a sniper rifle in your house and did your husband ever possess one in your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We never even saw it or had one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you have weapons in your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What kind of guns did you have in your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had hunting weapons, and it was a Carbine and a shotgun which we owned for seven or eight years, and we have the proof for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You, your husband and your family had in fact a permit for those guns, a permit that was issued by the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I could have exhibit 213 placed on the ELMO, with the assistance of the usher. Ms. Sahman, I am going to show you a copy of a permit. You have originally provided me with the original permit, and I am going to ask you if exhibit 213 is a true copy of the original that you showed to me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you. You also indicated -- let me turn now to the next day, which is 25th January 1993. You said around 6.00 in the morning, some sirens or alarms went off at nearby factories?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the Mediapan factory and the Vatrostalna company and the brick works.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: After that alarm went off at that particular factory, shooting started, did it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, for two days there was a lot of shooting. The bullets did not hit our house, they were going in different directions, in the vicinity of the camp; that is where they went. There were some red bullets flying there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were those bullets flying from the direction of the camp to the direction of the village of Strane?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in that area. I do not know if it was exactly from the camp, but it was in that direction in the area of Strane.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You observed bullets coming from that direction, around the camp, going into the village of Strane?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: After that firing the weapon, firing for two days, you said it sort of died down. Thereafter, the HVO came to your house on a number of occasions on the following days and continued to ask for the sniper; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The people who came to your house, how were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They all had camouflage uniforms with the HVO insignia and the chequer boards.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When they came to your house looking for the sniper, did they help themselves to some of your personal property?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were taking whatever they wanted. They would carry it out in their arms and we said, let them just take it away, but they were taking things.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you give them permission to take those items, or were they stealing those items from your home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were not even asked. They came in and they did whatever they wanted. We just stood there, they did not ask us for any permission, they just did what they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You testified yesterday, Ms. Sahman, that eventually your husband went to the village of Strane and spoke to a gentleman by the name of Ivica Andrijasevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Andrijasevic, yes. Yes, he talked to him and he asked for protection. He said that on the radio waves, there was word that there were some snipers there and he went down to the Cafe Sunce. Then all in the HVO uniforms, they were walking around the house and they told him, "Sit down, nobody will do anything to you." He came back into the house and we just sat there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr.. Andrijasevic was a member of the HVO as far as you knew; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was, yes. He was there around the Putis area, that is where he is from. He had control over that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Ms. Sahman, I would like to turn your attention to the theft of your car which occurred a number of days later. You indicated that a number of people came to your house and they took your car away. Can you describe what they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They also were wearing the camouflage uniforms and they had the chequer boards. They did not have the HVO insignia, they had something else on their sleeves. They came, they said they needed the car, they knew we had one, they knew everything. It was not somebody at random who came. My husband took it out of the garage and he said, "Do not turn it off", and he was strong, you know, but he just let them take it. My son started crying and he told him, "Do not worry, son, we will buy another one." Then some got into the car and some were in my brother-in-law's house. They had their own car, a Golf. They usually had the Golf cars, red and white and other colours, so that is how they left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please do not force the witness to repeat that she has said. She already spoke about the uniforms already. If the Defence challenges it, we can come back to that. Let us try to remain with points that in your opinion were not really made that clear. We have already heard about the child crying and the stolen car.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ms. Sahman, I would like to have if I could exhibit 212 placed on the ELMO. I am going to be asking you some questions, Ms. Sahman, about the events relating to your husband being taken from your home by the HVO and being taken to Kaonik camp. This is an exhibit you have seen yesterday, Ms. Sahman. Let me ask you some questions about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There is a number 3 circled on that particular exhibit, and, first off, let me ask you: is that an area that you can see from your home which is circled and numbered number 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: While your husband was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I could see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: While your husband was incarcerated, while he was imprisoned at Kaonik camp, you could see people in the area of 3 digging trenches; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did see that they were doing something, and later he came and he told me, "We are working here, we are digging trenches."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In fact he was escorted by a HVO soldier from that area to your house one of the days he was in custody; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He came and he put his hands behind his back and he was escorted by a soldier with the camouflage uniform, the HVO insignia and the chequer board. He just came home and we did not know what he was up to and he said, "It is not that good, but we are just working."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Ms. Sahman, there is a road that goes from the Busovaca T-junction, past number 3 and continues on. Do you see that road on that particular exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Is that the road that goes toward Busovaca and Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If you were going to travel from the village of Vitez, you would travel on the road that is indicated at the lower right-hand corner of exhibit 212, up to the Busovaca T-junction, turn right and go past number 3 and on to the direction of Busovaca and Kiseljak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your husband was eventually released from Kaonik camp on 8th February 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was released.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I could have exhibit 214 placed on the ELMO, I am going to ask you, Ms. Sahman, if you could identify what Prosecutor's exhibit 214 is. Can you recognise Prosecutor's exhibit 214 and can you tell the judges what it is, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise it. This is a certificate of the release from the camp on 8th February when my husband came back, so this is what we got. It says that it is under the auspices, but then nothing of that turned out to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention to the events that took place after your husband was murdered. You said that after your husband was murdered, you went to see a man by the name of Maric.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you tell us, was Mr.. Maric in the HVO, and if so, what part of the HVO was he in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was in the HVO, with the police. He had a white belt for a while, he wore those. There are several brothers there, Josip Maric and a younger one and the others were there less, but those two were there quite a bit. We saw them a number of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you tell Mr.. Maric about the events that had taken place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I came there and I told him that I was seeking protection. I told them, whenever I go to the village and go back, I would find the house broken into, but you know, they knew all this, they knew. They told me, "We cannot give you anything. Why do you not just stay there and nobody will do anything?" I said, "We did stay there and look what happened to me." He just kept silent, but I said, "Okay, I have no other choice", so I went back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Ms. Sahman, now I am going to show you two photographs. You and I have had an opportunity to talk about these particular photographs before coming into court and you have indicated to me that you would feel strong enough to identify the persons in these photographs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And you wanted these photographs to be shown to the court; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: First of all if I could have exhibit 215 placed on the ELMO? Ms. Sahman, can you identify the individual who is underneath the arrow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can; that is my husband.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you. You also indicated, Ms. Sahman, that you had family members who were killed in the village of Ahmici on 16th April 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I could have Prosecutor's Exhibit 110/2 placed on the ELMO, I am going to ask you if you can identify, Ms. Sahman, the members of your family who were killed in Ahmici on 16th April. Starting at the top picture with the two individuals seated on a couch, if we could focus on that first? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is my late father.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. If we could now move up and focus on the three individual photos; who are those men in those photographs, Ms. Sahman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My brother, late Nazif, who was born in 1950, my brother Rasim, who was born in 1964 and my brother Asim, who was born in 1954.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All of those people lost their lives in Ahmici on the 16th; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I also have a nephew who was also killed by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sahman. Now let me ask you one last question. Can you tell the judges why you fled to Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I fled because of the HVO, because we were terrorised by them. We could not live there any more. We held out as long as we could, and in the end I gave up, left everything behind and went to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Ms. Sahman, thank you very much for your testimony. Mr.. President, I would move into evidence Prosecutor's exhibits 212 through 215.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No objection, therefore it will be admitted into evidence. Madam Sahman, as the Prosecutor has certainly told you, you will now be asked some questions by the Defence counsel of the accused, that is of General Blaskic. I think it is going to be Mr.. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr.. President. Ms. Sahman, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You told the Prosecutor during the examination-in-chief that your husband never had a sniper, that he only had hunter weapons. Ms. Sahman, do you remember that you gave to an organisation called Ajid a statement in Zenica in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What kind of statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you remember that you made a statement for them referring to the same things that you have testified to now here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What does "perhaps" mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did make a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr.. Nobilo, can you be more precise with the question? I did not understand it very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: My question was whether on 10th May 1993, the lady made a statement regarding the same events that she has described here in the Tribunal for the organisation called Ajid, the secret service of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So did you make that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what organisation it was, but I did make some statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I will read to you a part of that statement, and then I will also show you your signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Will you please confirm it, if you can remember? You say in that statement: "My husband Fadil was a member of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He had with him hunting weapons and in the Army he was issued a sniper." Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had hunting weapons from before and he has the permits for them, for eight or nine years. As for the Army, I do not know what he had there. He went to the front-lines against the Chetniks at Turbe once and what he was issued there I do not know. I do not know, because we never saw a sniper, nor did he have one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I should like to ask the usher to show the witness this statement, so that she can confirm whether it is her signature or not. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I would like to tender this exhibit into evidence, and we can have it photocopied during the break for your Honours. The source is the Prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Ms. Sahman, your house, how far was it from the checkpoint in metres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, I never measured it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But roughly could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. It was not far, but I do not know how far.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How far is it from the intersection with Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is not far away either, it is all nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When the military policemen came, were they correct in their behaviour when they collected the rifles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They rang the bell, my husband asked who it was, the answer was, "The HVO police". He opened the door and they immediately pointed the pistol at him and asked for weapons and he said, "What weapons?", and they said, "Weapons", and he said, "Whatever I have has been mine for a long time, I have nothing else." They said, "But we need that too", and this one kept the pistol pointed at his chest all the time. Another one said, "Why do you not shoot him? Why are you wasting your time with him?", and that in itself was frightening enough. He asked for something in writing. They would not give him anything and then they said, "Just tell them that it is Miro from Kacuni that took the rifles."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you agree with my allegation that Ivica Andrijasevic was a HVO commander for the village of Jelinak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were some kind of branches, but I do not really know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Earlier on when you made your statement, you said that Ivica Andrijasevic was a HVO commander for the village of Jelinak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When my husband talked to him, then he said, "Do not worry, nobody will hurt you", because he is somebody with a position, something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You told the Prosecutor that you did not dare go to see your husband who was digging a trench at Vlatko's house, so my question is: why were you afraid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How could we dare walk in that direction when there was no one there. There were only the HVO people in uniform? I was afraid to go, I did not dare, I did not have the courage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But what were you afraid of? Was there any shooting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before there was and there was not a living soul there, except for them. Of course you had to be afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: For how many days was your husband at Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the camp? For four nights; we counted that. Four nights he spent there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And during these events in the village of Strane, was the village intact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All the men were taken to the Kaonik camp. They were driven away every morning from the village of Strane to the camp, to the Kaonik camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: During the investigation, you said that Maric was in the police station.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the former medical clinic, but I saw from my house that they gathered there often. I would see people going in and out, so I thought they must be there and I found him there. I asked him to help me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did he carry out an investigation on the spot where your husband was killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, nobody did anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you ask him to leave Busovaca and he refused to let you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where could we go there? We have no one to go to there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But did you ask for permission to leave Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not, I did not know who I would go to for that permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could the Registry please let me have the statement that we have just tendered into evidence? No, it is all right, I have a copy here. In that same statement, you said: "They would not let us move out."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had no one to ask, and we did not ask. I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So that was not correct, what you said in that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there was nothing we could do except decide for ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: My question is: was that true or not, what you said in your statement? The question is: did you ask and did they prevent you from moving out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not ask, we did not ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you report to the police that your car, TV sets and other things were stolen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Who could we report it to? No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, that is all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Prosecutor, any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Just a few, Mr. President. I asked you on direct examination, Ms. Sahman, whether or not you had ever seen a sniper rifle in your house, and your answer was no, you never did.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you another question, Ms. Sahman: was there an HVO barricade near your house as you were asked by Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Coming from the front-lines at Turbe, if you know, were there other HVO barricades along the road that led from, say, Novi Travnik to the Busovaca T-junction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was where the junction -- at the junction there was a barricade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If your husband travelled from the direction of Turbe with a sniper rifle, would he have to have crossed through the HVO barricade that was manned near your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he would have to pass there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. I turn to Judge Shahabuddeen; do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Witness, I have one or two questions. Some people came to your home and they asked whether you had a sniper. I am a little unclear in my own head as to whether you meant that they were asking whether you had a sniper weapon or whether they were asking whether you had a person shooting a sniper weapon. What was it they were asking for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They asked us about a sniper, "Do you have a sniper?" We said: no, and we never did have one. You can ask our other neighbours, Croats, those that my husband went hunting with, but they said, "Never mind", but later on we heard that there were reports that there was a sniper firing from behind our house, and then my husband went with Ivica Andrijasevic to look around and then he said that was just a trick and he came back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do I understand you then to be saying that they were asking whether you had a sniper weapon in your home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, when they came to our house, they were just asking for a sniper rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So we are agreed, we understand each other. All the weapons in your home were given up to the HVO police, and in particular to a man who called himself, I think, Miro from Kacuni; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: After all those weapons were given up, did the HVO still come back to your home and ask you for a sniper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was the first word they uttered, "Give us that sniper; why do you not surrender it for heaven's sake?", and he would say, "But I do not have it."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Now I will ask the Registrar to show you exhibit 213. There is something there which perhaps you can help me understand. Perhaps, Mr. Usher, you could light it up on the machine? Now look at the bottom left-hand section; do you see that? Look at the line headed by the word "Calibre". Look at the left-hand side of that line. Tell me, what is that word? I just do not know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean from the top? It says hunting Carbine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you see a line marked "Calibre", the third line from the very bottom, the bottom left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where it says "Snajper"? Is that what you are asking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. Is that the same word as the sniper which was being talked about, or does it mean something different there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, then it would be indicated that he had a sniper. You see there is a list of what he had, first a hunting rifle and the Carbine. People could get a sniper, but we did not have one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The correct understanding then is that that line is saying, with the dash or slash, "No sniper"; is that what it is saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it says. "No sniper."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I see. Now I understand you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Ms. Sahman, your testimony is over. The judges wish to thank you for being very courageous to describe these tragic events to us. You can go back home now, under the protection of the Witness and Victims Unit, and how are we going to proceed Mr. Registrar now? Are we going to bring down the blinds so that the witness can be accompanied out?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, we have to close the blinds just to allow the witness to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please stay seated for the moment so that we provide full protection for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President and your Honours, good afternoon. We will turn to our next witness, who also is a protected witness, and I believe the letter designation for this witness is Witness U, as in "uniform". To lay out the basis as to where this particular individual fits into the indictment, I will set forth the preliminary facts as follows. Before I begin, I did address this particular issue concerning Witness U and the protections that Witness U requires with counsel prior to the session and they have concurred to a pseudonym, Witness U, and also protection for face and body. With regard to the testimony of Witness U, as your Honours heard yesterday from Witness T, there was a significant amount of trench-digging and beating that took place in the Kaonik camp, commencing the latter part of January 1993 and going on until approximately February 7th or 8th 1993. Witness U's testimony will begin, your Honours, with the actual trench-digging that took place and testimony concerning the beatings. What Witness U will tell you is, without repeating the testimony of Witness T, what actually took place, because Witness U was one of the individuals who was not only incarcerated in Kaonik camp commencing on 30th January 1993 but he was also taken out to four different locations in and around the Busovaca-Kaonik area, where he was forced to dig trenches under the watchful eye of HVO troops under the command of the accused. He will also testify concerning the beatings that took place at these locations. As Witness T told you previously, there was much discussion about particular individuals having been beaten while digging trenches. Witness U will testify that in the dead of night, he could hear those witnesses screaming as they were being beaten. He will likewise testify as to their release, and that is just a short sketch of the testimony of Witness U concerning the trench-digging. Witness U will also testify as to the choices that were given to him concerning where he could go upon his release from the Kaonik jail. He was given the alternative of going to Zenica, Kacuni and Busovaca. However, he was told by the HVO that should he choose to go to Busovaca, there was no guarantee that he could be safe and they could not guarantee his safety. So with this Hobson's choice, he, of course, went to Zenica. Thereafter he will testify that he went to another location, a village where he currently resides. However his family, his father, mother, grandfather, brother, cousin, remained in the Busovaca area and on 27th April 1993, or late on 26th April 1993, his father who was an invalid, his grandfather and his cousin were executed by a member of the HVO called Zoran Marinic, known as Svabo, and that his mother was wounded and his mother was thereafter taken to Travnik. With regard to the particular charges that these facts will be directed to in the indictment, naturally these charges begin with the persecution of the Muslim population, because what Witness U will tell you is that during the time-frame that he was in the Kaonik camp from late January to approximately 8th February, approximately 400 Muslims were incarcerated at that location and taken out to dig trenches and other types of manual labour, in addition to being beaten. These charges obviously go to the persecution charge themselves, the inhumane treatment of civilians, that is set forth in the persecution charge in 6.2 and 6.4, as well as 6.5. Concerning the actual counts themselves, his testimony will be directed towards count 5 through 10, wilful killing of civilians. His testimony will also be directed towards the inhumane treatment of hostages that is set forth in counts 15 through 20, and if your Honours focus in on paragraph 12 in counts 15 through 20, you will note that the Kaonik camp is listed second from the top as one of the locations where these individuals were incarcerated and counts 13, 14 et cetera, mostly counts 13 and 14, delineate the fashion in which this particular individual was treated contrary to law and his facts will support counts through 20. That is basically a thumbnail sketch of what Witness U will testify to and it will be a continuing follow-up of the events that took place in Busovaca in January 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. Things are clear now; we can have the witness brought in. This will be a public hearing, the blinds will be raised once the witness has taken the oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just as a preliminary matter, an exhibit that I think we can address at this juncture is yet another overhead of the Busovaca area that has not been previously submitted into evidence. I have given a copy to counsel, Mr. Dubuisson has the copies that are before him. This particular exhibit, and I believe this is exhibit 216, Mr. Dubuisson.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is another Rule 70 exhibit that was provided by the United Kingdom and, consistent with Rule 70, it has been previously given to counsel. So at this juncture, Mr. President, we would offer exhibit 216 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: No additional comments other than our general comments on these aerial photos that we have previously stated, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think that we had reserved the decision that we were rendering for the time being. The Tribunal will give its decision at the proper time. But whatever the decision the Tribunal is going to take, we may not have to talk about this document. We can have the witness brought in. We will have to talk about it. (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you hear me? First you will identify your name, without stating it, as it appears on the piece of Registrar that the Registrar is showing to you. Be sure it is correct, but do not say it. Also, please remain seated to take your solemn declaration, which in fact is your oath. Please read the sentence which is on the paper. WITNESS U (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness U. This is the name we are going to give you. Since you are benefiting from protective measures taken by the Tribunal in agreement with the Defence and the Prosecution. Please concentrate your statement, after a few preliminary questions asked by the Prosecutor. You have been asked to appear as a Prosecution witness in the trial of General Blaskic. Once you have made your statement, we will speak about the digging of the trenches, the detention conditions, the conditions under which you were released and the conditions under which members of your family were murdered. Mr. Prosecutor, this is how we are limiting the discussion; you ask a few questions and then let the witness talk. Go ahead, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, thank you. Good afternoon, Witness U.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Witness U, how old are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Are you of the Muslim religion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Prior to 30th January 1993, did you live in the village of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you live in the village of Busovaca with your father, mother, grandfather, brother, cousins and other members of your family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Fighting began in Bosnia in April 1992, and thereafter, did you join the Territorial Defence and go fight on the front-lines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Where did you fight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At Visoko.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How many times did you go to the front-line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you go any time after that one time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was in July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Witness U, fighting began in Busovaca on 25th January 1993, did it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Where were you at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Between 25th and 29th January, I was in a house together with my family and other neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What were you doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were in a shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you actually engaged in fighting members of the HVO between 25th and 29th January 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention to 30th January 1993. Did HVO soldiers come to your area, which I think is approximately about 2 kilometres from downtown Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they came, between eight and ten of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In your own words, Witness U, tell the judges what happened when they came, where they took you, what happened when you got to Kaonik Prison; tell the judges in your own words, if you could, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 30th January, they arrived at around midday, about eight or ten of them. They wore camouflage uniforms. They asked me to give them the automatic rifle, because they knew I was a member of the Territorial Defence. I did not have the rifle. Our weapons were at the front-lines where the exchanges were taking place. They also asked this of others. Then they lined us up, we were 18, in front of my house and they took us towards the centre of Busovaca. Near the Sumarija, they searched us, then they loaded us on to a minibus and took us in the direction of the Kaonik barracks. They brought us in there, and put us all in a single cell. We found there another two persons. After a while, they started calling out the names and they were taking us to another room which was also in that same building. They were asking about rifles, that is the weapons. The questioning took about ten to fifteen minutes, and then they took us back to the cells, but not to the same cell. On that day, none of us went anywhere. The next day, they started calling people out, and 30 of us were called out. They loaded us on to a truck of the Rab make, it was yellow colour, and took us in the direction of Prosije. There we dug trenches until late in the evening. We received no food and no water. During those eight days in the camp, I was at Prosije, at Kula, Kovacevac. The last night in the camp, on the way back from Kula, just as we were coming back, I heard of the murder of Jasmin Sehovic and Nermin Elezovic. I found this out at the barracks. That same day in the morning around 8.00, the Red Cross vehicles arrived and the exchange took place, and I went in the direction of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. President, if I can clarify some issues concerning this time-frame before we move to the April time-frame, it may speed things along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Witness U, you said that on 30th January, soldiers came to your village and arrested 18 men; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were these HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You said they had camouflage uniforms. Did they have any insignia on their shoulders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they had the HVO insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the 18 men that were arrested, were they all Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the HVO soldiers that arrested you and the other 17 men, did you recognise any of those HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I recognised two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Who were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dario Lastro, who went to school with me, and Marinko Jevresak, whom I know by sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can turn your attention to an exhibit and I believe that exhibit is now 217, your Honours, if I could ask that this not be put on the ELMO, simply because it designates his residence. If I could give that to counsel and your Honours and one to the witness. Witness U, you have seen this photograph before, have you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The number up in the upper right-hand corner, the number 1, is that your residence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If you follow the green line down to number 2, is that the path that you followed when the HVO soldiers took you and 17 other men to the centre of town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What time of day was this when this arrest took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some time in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So it was broad daylight outside; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You said you were taken to the centre of town after you were paraded into town and you were searched. Would that be at the point, that is number 2, on the main road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thereafter, did you follow this green line down to the Kaonik camp in the minibus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you got to the Kaonik camp, did you see any HVO soldiers manning the gate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were they military policemen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How did you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Then you said when you went inside, you began to be questioned again concerning where weapons were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After we were taken to the office, that is to the cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Who questioned you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zarko Petrovic and Marko Krilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were they likewise members of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most likely they were, they were wearing camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: After they questioned you, you said you were put in a cell. Can you describe the cell to the judges and how many other people were in this cell with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The cell measured 3 by 2, I believe, 3 by 2 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So the cell was 3 metres by 2 metres.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Could everybody lay down and sleep at night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they could not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you given bread, blankets and water to sustain you in January weather?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not receive blankets, we got bread and water.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Correct me, there were approximately 20 people in this 3 by 2 cell with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depended on the cell. Somewhere there were 15 people, somewhere there were 20, somewhere even 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You also mentioned that you were taken out to dig trenches and you mentioned various locations and I would like to turn your attention to exhibit 218, which is an excerpt of Exhibit 29, your Honours. Mr. Dubuisson, if you want me to use a letter on this, or just give it another exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is 218.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We can put that on the ELMO, if your Honours want. Sir, you have seen this map and these locations before because you and I have spoken about these locations, have we not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You noted in your testimony that you went out to dig trenches on the first day; is that right? After you stayed there, the next day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next day, the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Where was that? Can you use the pointer and point to it on the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What town is that, or village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Milavice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What did you do there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were fixing up the dugouts there, we were connecting the dugouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was this a military installation that you were digging dugouts for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, those were military structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Who was guarding you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Soldiers who held the front-line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were these HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think you noted that at this location, you received no food, although you worked all day; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not receive any.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Using that map and the pointer, tell the court the next location where you dug trenches.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Prosije.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Could you point to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What did you do there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Same types of work as in Milavice. We dug dugouts and we covered them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So this was another military installation that you were working on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Some time around this time, did the Red Cross come and visit you and other people that were in jail at Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think they visited us on the second or third day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were people taken out to dig trenches that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How about in the evening after the Red Cross left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some were called out, which meant that they went somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But you were not; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn our attention to the next day: did you continue to dig trenches the next day after the ICRC came?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you recall where that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure whether it was Milavice or Kovacevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You picked Milavice, but did you dig trenches at some time also at Kovacevac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you point to that location on the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What did you do at Kovacevac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We also dug dugouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Another military installation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you go to Milavice on more than one occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How about Kovacevac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Those are three locations and you mentioned a fourth location that you went to dig trenches; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Kula.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Using exhibit 218, could you point Kula out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Tell the judges about Kula. What were you digging in Kula, how many men were digging there and what were the conditions for the prisoners such as yourself digging there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We arrived at Kula in the evening hours, the 30 of us, and as we were arriving, we were being assigned to dig trenches. I was among the first, so that I stayed almost at the start, which was -- we were spaced about 10 to 15 metres apart and we dug trenches there. There were people there who had come before us, and they were engaged in the same work that we were. Late in the evening, around midnight, we could hear some shouting, which meant that somebody was being beaten. We dug for about two or three hours, and then a truck arrived. They put us on it and they drove us in the direction of Kaonik. The first group had been taken there before us, so that when we arrived in the barracks, we saw that they had been beaten up. They were bloodied, but we could not stop. They immediately took us to our cells, so that we just had a glimpse of them. That was the last night in Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: During this night, you heard yelling. Did you hear any of these men screaming?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did they tell you how they were being beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the next day during the exchange they told us how they were beaten. They forced a prisoner to go from one to the other and hit them with the shovel handle and if he did not do it, then they would beat him up and they would tell him how he should hit them. They told us about the killings of Elezovic -- Jasmin Sehovic and Nermin Elezovic, who were there digging.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were these HVO soldiers that were guarding these prisoners and you in Kula the night before you were released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were HVO soldiers with you when you were digging trenches in Kula?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you were digging trenches in Kula, was someone -- were there HVO soldiers on the line there with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were there HVO -- was it an HVO soldier or soldiers who were forcing these Muslim men to beat each other in Kula, when you heard the screams?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most probably it was them who did force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That was the night before you were released; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On the day you were released, and that was 8th February 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 8th or 9th, I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On the day that you were released, did you see how many Muslim men were being held in jail in Kaonik when the exchange was supposed to take place? Did you see the number of Muslim men there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I saw a large mass. The number was somewhere between 400 and 420 prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were they all Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the most part, they were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: At that point, did you see some of these men that had been beaten the night before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You told the judges that you went to Zenica after you were released. Did the HVO give you a choice as to where you wanted to go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did. We had a choice of Zenica, Busovaca, Kacuni. They told us that they could not guarantee safety in Busovaca, which meant that we could only go to Kacuni or to Zenica. Some on their own went to Skradno.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Witness U, who told you that your safety could not be guaranteed in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The personnel in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were these HVO personnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Witness U, you decided to go to Zenica. Do you know Muslim men who went back to Busovaca who were harmed after they went back to Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know whether people were injured, but I know who went.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did they stay there, Witness U, or did they ultimately leave Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the end, they had to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Witness U, let me move to the events of 27th April 1993. I know you were not there, but can you tell the judges what happened to your family on 27th April.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 27th April 1993, in the evening, about 10.00 or 10.30 pm, Zoran, known as Svabo came with another unknown person to me, to my house, and asked my family about a radio transmitter and asked Ramiz Hodzic. These were the two families that had stayed behind. They searched the upper floor and set fire to it. He left the house looking for Ramiz Hodzic again, and as he could not find him, he came back to my house and then, using his gun, he killed my father, my grandfather, my brother, my cousin; and my mother was wounded. Half an hour later UNPROFOR arrived. My mother, my cousin and my brother were transferred to the clinic in Busovaca. My father and grandfather succumbed to their injuries on the spot. In the clinic in Busovaca, my brother died from his injuries, then my cousin and mother were transferred to Travnik. On the 28th at 3.00 am, my cousin died, but my mother survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Witness U, how old was your grandfather?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was born in 1908.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How about your father; when was he born and what was his physical condition at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My father was born on 14th February 1945. He was totally disabled, an invalid 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And your brother?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My brother was born on 21st April 1977.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you know when your cousin was born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 9th January 1975.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This took place on 27th April 1993, and it took place in your house that you previously described in exhibit 217. By that time, had most of the Muslims that lived in that area left the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only two families stayed behind, my own and the family of Ramiz Hodzic. The rest had left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You noted that the individual that did this was Zoran. Was that Zoran Marinic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zoran Marinic, known as Svabo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you know this man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How did you know him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His uncle lived in our immediate vicinity, about 100 or 150 metres away, so I would see him there, and also I know him from downtown; he worked as a house painter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: At this point, did you know if Zoran Marinic, Svabo, was a member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him when he escorted the prisoners to Prosije. That was when I saw him for the first time in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In fact, Witness U, he escorted you and other prisoners to dig trenches in Prosije, did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, only when we went to Prosije.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can turn your attention at this point to our last exhibit which is exhibit 218, which is two photographs, the top photograph being 218/1 and the second photograph 219. Because the witness is a protected witness, your Honours, I would just like to allow him to look at the two photographs and describe his family members that are in the two photographs respectively. He has provided these and is willing to attest to his family members that are in these two photographs. If we could turn to the first photograph, Witness U, exhibit 219/1, the one you are looking at with the many members of your family -- yes, that one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Are any of your family members that were executed on the evening of 27th April 1993 in this photo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there are. My father and my brother, and my mother who was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Moving from right to left, which individual is your father?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The one in the red pullover.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And your brother?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In front of him, wearing a light blue jacket and a pack on his back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That is the young boy, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Behind the young boy and next to your father with the red pullover is your mother; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn to the next photograph, which is 219/2. Are any of your family members that were executed on 27th April in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are, there is my grandfather.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is he the individual, the man who is second from the left with the brown jacket on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour at this time, your Honours, I have no further questions of this witness. If I might just consult with my colleagues for one moment? (Pause). Your Honour at this time we will offer into evidence exhibits 216, 217, 218 and 219, and the request at this juncture, because it is a protected witness, is that exhibit 217, the map with the witness's home designated, and, of course, the photographs, 219, be placed under seal. With those caveats, your Honour, we have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No objection from the Defence. Who now has the floor, Mr. Nobilo or Mr. Hayman? It is Mr. Nobilo, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, Witness U. In the examination-in-chief, you told the Prosecutor that fighting occurred as of 25th January 1993, and that the fighting went on until 29th January 1993. I would like to know where those battles took place, how far away from your house? Where was the front-line, the line of conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fighting could be heard at Kadica Strane, which is about 2 or 3 kilometres from my house as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I will read a part of the statement that you gave early on to members of the Office of the Prosecution, so please confirm or deny it. You said: "The attack started on 25th or 26th February 1993, on Sunday afternoon at 3.00. The Ustashas came from the town of Busovaca." Let me repeat: "The attack started on 25th or 26th January 1993 on a Sunday afternoon at 3.00 pm. The Ustashas came from the town of Busovaca, and they were moving towards Kacuni in an armoured vehicle. Our soldiers started to defend themselves by returning the fire using a hand-grenade launcher. There was no conflict in the town of Busovaca itself, but there was fighting along the front-lines in the woods that were 500 metres to 5 kilometres from the town. Our soldiers put up resistance in a locality, in Kadica Strana which is about 200 metres from the centre of Busovaca." Is all that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How many days did you spend in Kaonik exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From 30th January until the 8th or 9th; I am not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who did you hear from that Sehovic and Elezovic had been killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the prisoners at Kula.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you give us the name of that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not like to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that you were exchanged. Who were you exchanged with? How shall I put it. For whom were you exchanged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were Croats that had been captured in the area of Kacuni.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Were they Croat civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was an intervention squad; that is how we were told in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And how many Croats were there that were captured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: While you were working on the dugouts, did you see nearby soldiers of the BH-Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not see them, but we were shown where the front-line of the BH-Army was, or rather of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you see any single soldier in that direction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We saw some in the area of Kovacevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did the BH-Army fire at you, in your direction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that your family was executed by Zoran Marinic, called Svabo. You did not see that. Who described this to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Is it the same Marinic Zoran called Svabo who has been indicted by this Tribunal for those acts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: That is all, Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Are there any additional questions that you would like to ask in relation to the cross-examination, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just one, Mr. President. The questions that you were just asked on cross-examination concerning the beginning of the attack on 25th January, you were not present when those attacks took place, were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Riad?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You told us about the sad execution of your father, grandfather and brother. To your knowledge, what was the charge, why were they executed? If you want to give me a bigger picture. Were they fighting back, was there a quarrel, a battle between them and between that Zoran Marinic, or was it a cold-blooded execution? What was the reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware of any reason. They themselves did not know why they came; probably because those two houses were the only ones left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What happened to the other houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The people had abandoned them before that, they had fled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This Zoran Marinic, if you know, was he acting on his own, or was it some kind of official attitude or organised way of executing people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: One question. The Prosecutor was asking you about some people who went to Busovaca and who later on had to leave Busovaca, and I think he was interested in finding out from you why they had to leave Busovaca. Your answer, I took it down, was this: "At the end, they had to leave." What did you mean by that, that they had to leave? Why did they have to leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because they were collecting them again to dig and complete the work on the dugouts, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Who was collecting them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness U. You have finished your testimony and the Tribunal thanks you for having come to The Hague to tell what you experienced, which is very painful for you and we hope that you will be able to return home under peaceful conditions and that you will be able to try to get beyond everything that has happened. Thank you very much for having come. Please do not move, you are a protected witness. The judges will suspend the hearing now for a half-hour break, and the witness will be able to leave once the judges have left the courtroom. (4.20 pm) (A short break) (4.50 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will resume the hearing. Have the accused brought in, please. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I sigh that it is still a protected witness; is that correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In part, Mr. President, the next witness is Dr. Zahid Beganovic. Dr. Beganovic, who is the Director of the canton hospital in Zenica, merely wants facial distortion and name or identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Dr. Beganovic, and only face distortion. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President and your Honours. We are taking a shift in the factual presentation at this juncture. We will be moving back to some other additional facts in Busovaca later on in the week. However, because some of the witnesses have to get out of town et cetera, we have to move ahead in this area, somewhat out of sequence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What is the calendar for the week? Since you are raising this issue, we are meeting tomorrow morning from 10.00 until 1.00 and then on Friday. Are all your witnesses here, all those that you have for this week?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, they are. For instance Dr. Beganovic runs a rather large hospital facility and has requested to go back as soon as possible, so we are making a change in course and covering the shelling of Zenica, or beginning to cover the shelling of Zenica that took place on 19th April 1993. It is the Prosecutor's position that in the shelling of Zenica numerous civilians were killed and seriously injured and others slightly injured by HVO shelling about midday on 19th April 1993. Dr. Beganovic, who was a surgeon, an eye, ear and throat surgeon at the hospital at that time, shortly thereafter became the doctor of that hospital facility. He will testify to your Honours the serious injuries that were suffered, exactly what those injuries were, the number of those serious injuries and he will give a number of the slightly injured without going into the slightly injured in detail and a rough estimate of the number of civilians killed; however a subsequent witness will give a more exact figure on the number of individuals killed. With regard to the actual counts of the indictment that Dr. Beganovic and the next several witnesses will be addressing, are all those notations in the indictment regarding the city of Zenica, the attacks on cities, towns and villages and the killing of civilians and causing serious injury and the destruction and plunder of property, as reflected in the persecution count, count 1 of the indictment would be included in the testimony of Dr. Beganovic and the subsequent witnesses. Turning ourselves ahead to the unlawful attack on civilians and civilian objects in counts 2 and 4, your Honours can see that the city of Zenica is reflected in that count as well, so this testimony will be pertinent to those counts. As continuing on, it will also be pertinent to counts 5 and 10, the wilful killing and serious injury counts as set forth in the indictment. In substance, Mr. President, those are the counts to which these series of witnesses will be addressing themselves. I noted at the outset that we are moving somewhat out of order, moving into the Zenica shelling issue. Even in that sequence, Mr. President and your Honours, we are putting Dr. Beganovic on first because as I noted at the outset, he runs a pretty big hospital and simply must get back to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With that, Mr. President and your Honours, we have no further comments at this time and would move ahead with the testimony of Dr. Beganovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: About how long do you think this is going to take, this testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: He is going to tell us the serious injuries of about 18 witnesses, I believe. Given his qualifications it should be approximately half an hour to 45 minutes. I would not think it would be much longer than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right, Registrar, we can have Dr. Zahid Beganovic brought in. (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I believe that you can indicate your last name and first name for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My last name is Beganovic and the first name is Zahid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Can you please remain standing and read the solemn declaration that the usher is giving to you. DR. ZAHID BEGANOVIC (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, doctor. You may be seated. You have agreed to testify at the request of the Prosecutor in the case before this Tribunal against the accused who is present in this courtroom, General Blaskic. You, as a surgeon, at Zenica Hospital, you witnessed shelling which caused wounds and deaths about which you are going to speak. I believe that the Prosecutor will ask you some general questions and then you will testify, concentrating specifically on the essential points, at least those that you consider to be essential and which the Prosecution judges to be essential. Mr. Kehoe, the floor is yours if you want to ask some preliminary questions and then allow the witness to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: A practical question: do you have your glasses with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not. I left them behind, and I think that they should be brought in for me. I left them in my jacket.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Which means that the witness needed to have some documents before him. Perhaps he can speak without having any documents there to please the Defence. We will have to go and look for his glasses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Cayley just ran back to take a look at --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I think that I would be able to read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think I will ask a few preliminary questions concerning the doctor's qualifications and I think Mr. Cayley will be back during that period of time with the doctor's glasses. Doctor, if you can, can you tell us your position at this point and tell us about your medical career and where you studied medicine and what specialisations you focused on during your medical career and what you are doing now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I finished classical high school in Sarajevo in 1965. I enrolled in the School of Medicine at the University of Zagreb and I graduated by 1970, which is when I became a general practitioner. Then after my internship, I started practising in Zenica. After that, I enrolled in graduate studies in occupational medicine. When I completed my graduate studies and specialisation, I enrolled in the ENT surgery specialisation course in Ljubljana, which I completed in Ljubljana in 1980 and since that time, I worked as an ENT surgeon, that is surgeon for ear, nose and throat. During the war, I was in this position and at the head of the Crisis Staff which was established at the hospital so that they -- we could take better care of them. Since the fall of 1993, I have been on duty of the -- the Director of the canton hospital in Zenica. During the shelling of Zenica, I was the head of the Crisis Staff and on that day, I was the specialist for eyes, ears and nose on duty so that I personally received some of the patients who arrived on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
